title: 2024 Formal Ethics Opinion 1 — Use of Artificial Intelligence in a Law Practice
author: North Carolina State Bar

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: AI use is permitted subject to existing professional duties
kp.d: Adopted November 1, 2024, the North Carolina State Bar opinion permits AI use under existing professional rules rather than prescribing when and how lawyers should adopt it. It treats AI as a resource between conventional practice software and nonlawyer support, requiring competence, confidentiality, supervision and independent judgment. These are ethical requirements, not empirical findings about adoption.
qs: Nothing in the Rules of Professional Conduct specifically addresses, let alone prohibits, a lawyer’s use of AI in her law practice.

However, should a lawyer choose to employ AI in her practice, the lawyer must do so competently, the lawyer must do so securely, and the lawyer must exercise her independent judgment in supervising the use of such processes in her practice.

kp.k: Efficiency benefits coexist with unreliable outputs
kp.d: The opinion asserts that AI can improve efficiency and consistency across discovery, document review, research, contract drafting and data analysis, while warning that apparently reliable output may be inaccurate. Its scope includes extractive and generative AI; it notes that lawyers may already use AI through familiar research services. It does not quantify efficiency gains or error rates.
qs: It is unquestioned that AI can be used in the practice of law to increase efficiency and consistency in the provision of legal services.
However, AI and its work product can be inaccurate or unreliable despite its appearance of reliability when used during the provision of legal services.

From discovery and document review to legal research, drafting contracts, and aggregating/analyzing data trends, the possibilities for employing AI in a law practice are increasingly present and constantly evolving.

kp.k: Lawyers retain responsibility for verification and reliance
kp.d: Under Rule 1.1, lawyers must understand the benefits, risks and case-specific implications of the tools they employ. Rule 5.3 requires reasonable efforts to ensure third-party AI services are compatible with professional obligations. AI does not transfer responsibility away from the lawyer, who must review its work and independently decide whether to rely on it.
qs: Should a lawyer decide to employ AI in the representation of a client, however, the lawyer is fully responsible for the use and impact of AI in the client’s case.
Educational efforts include, but are not limited to, reviewing current and relevant resources on AI broadly and on the specific program intended for use during the provision of legal services.
the lawyer is individually responsible for reviewing, evaluating, and ultimately relying upon the work produced by someone—or something—other than the lawyer.

kp.k: Client information requires security diligence and separate privilege analysis
kp.d: Client documents and data may be supplied to third-party AI only after the lawyer is satisfied that security meets Rule 1.6(c). Reasonable precautions depend on circumstances, including information sensitivity and the costs or benefits of additional safeguards; absolute security is not demanded. The committee expressly leaves attorney-client privilege outside its ethical determination and directs lawyers to resolve privilege questions before use.
qs: Yes, provided the lawyer has satisfied herself that the third-party company’s AI program is sufficiently secure and complies with the lawyer’s obligations to ensure any client information will not be inadvertently disclosed or accessed by unauthorized individuals pursuant to Rule 1.6(c).

At the outset, the Ethics Committee does not opine on whether the information shared with an AI tool violates the attorney-client privilege, as the issue is a legal question and outside the scope of the Rules of Professional Conduct.

A lawyer should research and resolve any question on privilege prior to engaging with a third-party company’s AI program for use in the provision of legal services to a client, particularly if client-specific information will be provided to the AI program.

kp.k: Vendor diligence continues throughout AI use
kp.d: Drawing on 2011 FEO 6 and a proposed Florida Bar opinion, the committee identifies vendor reputation and stability, contractual security protections, retrieval or destruction arrangements, retention and proprietary claims as relevant checks. Lawyers should keep learning about selected tools, consult security professionals periodically and adjust or abandon services when their security becomes doubtful.
qs: Whether the terms of service clarify how information provided to the company will be retrieved by the lawyer or otherwise safely destroyed if not retrieved should the company go out of business, change ownership, or if services are terminated.
Furthermore, this duty of reasonable care continues beyond initial selection of a service, program, or tool and extends throughout the lawyer’s use of the service.

The aforementioned considerations—including the consideration regarding ownership of information articulated by the Florida Bar opinion—are equally applicable to a lawyer’s selection and use of a third party company’s AI service/program.

kp.k: Public AI raises client-data retention and training risks
kp.d: The opinion warns that some publicly available AI systems retain user inputs and train on them. It requires lawyers to investigate these practices and, expressly qualified to the date of the opinion, generally recommends avoiding client-specific inputs into public AI resources rather than asserting that every AI service has identical data practices.
qs: Importantly, some current AI programs are publicly available to all consumers/users, and the nature of the AI program is to retain and train itself based on the information provided by any user of its program.
Generally, and as of the date of this opinion, lawyers should avoid inputting client-specific information into publicly available AI resources.

kp.k: Local deployment does not eliminate confidentiality risks
kp.d: Running third-party-developed AI on firm-owned infrastructure does not change Rule 1.6(c) obligations. The opinion cautions that local servers may be more vulnerable than larger providers' infrastructure and recommends cybersecurity consultation. Customized systems may also transmit inputs back to a central public system, making operational understanding necessary before deployment.
qs: Lawyer remains responsible for keeping the information secure pursuant to Rule 1.6(c) regardless of the program’s location.

A lawyer who plans to independently store client information should consult an information technology/cybersecurity expert about steps needed to adequately protect the information stored on local servers.
some of these customized programs may continue to send information inputted into the firm-specific program back to the central program for additional use or training.

kp.k: AI-drafted pleadings carry unchanged professional accountability
kp.d: Signing an AI-assisted pleading does not reduce a lawyer's obligations. The opinion invokes the prohibition on frivolous proceedings in Rule 3.1 and the reasonable-inquiry certification under North Carolina Rule of Civil Procedure 11. Lawyers adopting AI output as their own remain professionally responsible for it.
qs: A lawyer may not abrogate her responsibilities under the Rules of Professional Conduct by relying upon AI.
A lawyer’s signature on a pleading also certifies the lawyer’s good faith belief as to the factual and legal assertions therein.
If the lawyer employs AI in her practice and adopts the tool’s product as her own, the lawyer is professionally responsible for the use of the tool’s product.

kp.k: Substantive AI delegation requires advance informed client consent
kp.d: Disclosure depends on the technology, intended output, reliance and individual representation under Rule 1.4(b). Ordinary research and practice-management uses generally need not be disclosed, but substantive delegation is treated as outsourcing requiring advance informed consent. Lawyers must also seek client input where an AI-use decision requires their participation concerning fees.
qs: Generally, a lawyer need not inform her client that she is using an AI tool to complete ordinary tasks, such as conducting legal research or generic case/practice management.

However, if a lawyer delegates substantive tasks in furtherance of the representation to an AI tool, the lawyer’s use of the tool is akin to outsourcing legal work to a nonlawyer or other third-party resource or service, for which the client’s advanced informed consent is required.
Additionally, if the decision to use or not use an AI tool in the case requires the client’s input with regard to fees, the lawyer must inform and seek input from the client.

kp.k: Hourly billing cannot recapture time saved by AI
kp.d: A hypothetical estate-planning lawyer charging $300 per hour reduces document preparation from approximately three hours to one hour using AI. The opinion prohibits billing three hours: this illustration is not a measured productivity result. Lawyers may instead benefit by serving more clients, or use a client-approved flat fee that is not clearly excessive.
qs: No, Lawyer may not bill a client for three hours of work when only one hour of work was actually experienced.
If the use of AI in Lawyer’s practice results in greater efficiencies in providing legal services, Lawyer may enjoy the benefit of those new efficiencies by completing more work for more clients;

Rather than billing on an hourly basis, Lawyer may consider billing clients a flat fee for the drafting of documents—even when using AI to assist in drafting—provided the flat fee charged is not clearly excessive and the client consents to the billing structure.

kp.k: AI expenses may be charged with safeguards
kp.d: The opinion permits charging clients for AI expenses when accurate, not clearly excessive and consented to, preferably in writing. Recoverable costs can include specifically identified, matter-related AI use or a general administrative fee covering technology expenses that improve service or client convenience.
qs: Relatedly, Lawyer may also bill a client for expenses incurred related to Lawyer’s use of AI in the furtherance of a client’s legal services, provided the expenses charged are accurate, not clearly excessive, and the client consents to the charge, preferably in writing.
a lawyer’s use of AI that is specifically identified and directly related to the legal services provided to the client during the representation;

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The North Carolina State Bar describes AI as capable of improving efficiency and consistency across legal tasks, but permits its use only with continuing lawyer responsibility, confidentiality safeguards and supervision.
pts.d: The opinion identifies research, discovery, document review, contract drafting and data analysis as applications. It warns that apparently reliable output can be inaccurate: lawyers must check and exercise independent judgment over work they adopt, and AI does not change their responsibility for signed pleadings. It also identifies confidentiality risks from providers retaining inputs for training and cautions that local hosting does not necessarily provide better security. Substantive delegation to AI requires advance informed client consent, unlike ordinary research or practice-management uses. On the business model, AI efficiencies cannot justify charging hourly clients for time not worked; lawyers may instead benefit through additional client work or consensual, non-clearly-excessive flat fees. These are the State Bar's descriptions and ethical conclusions, not predictions of employment displacement or quantified market change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source principally relies on professional-conduct authority and analogies to existing technology and outsourcing obligations, rather than empirical performance or market evidence.
pts.d: The State Bar grounds its conclusions in North Carolina professional-conduct rules on competence, confidentiality, supervision, communication, fees and honesty, together with prior ethics opinions and North Carolina Civil Procedure Rule 11. It cites a proposed Florida opinion for vendor information-retention considerations. Background references include explanatory technology resources and commentary on AI in law. A news report about lawyers citing bogus AI-generated case law supports the warning about unreliable output; it is not a measured hallucination rate. No benchmark or systematic productivity study is supplied. The estate-planning example of drafting time falling from three hours to one at $300 per hour is a hypothetical inquiry used to explain billing duties, not an observed productivity result.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The opinion addresses current practice as of its adoption on November 1, 2024, with ongoing, context-dependent obligations rather than a forecast deadline.
pts.d: The background describes generative AI's growth in capability and popularity during the preceding year. Permission to use AI is conditional on competence, security and supervision; the source expressly declines to prescribe when and how adoption is appropriate. Vendor due diligence must continue throughout use, with adjustments or abandonment if security concerns emerge. The advice generally to avoid client-specific inputs into publicly available AI is explicitly qualified as of the opinion's date. Client disclosure depends on the technology, task and reliance: ordinary research generally needs no notice, while substantive outsourcing requires advance informed consent. Fees must reflect actual time when billed hourly; flat fees and AI-related expense charges are subject to consent and limits on excessiveness. Attorney-client privilege is expressly left unresolved as a legal question to research before use.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The opinion addresses lawyers and firms using AI, their clients, and third-party technology providers, without predicting differential effects by firm size or legal-market segment.
pts.d: Lawyers remain responsible for competence, verification of output, vendor selection, data protection and billing even when technology performs part of the work. Firms running AI on their own infrastructure retain the same confidentiality obligations and may need cybersecurity expertise. Clients are affected through output reliability, protection of confidential information, participation in substantive delegation decisions and accurate charges. The hypothetical estate-planning practitioner illustrates how efficiency affects hourly billing and possible flat-fee arrangements. Third-party AI companies are treated as software or service providers whose compatibility with professional duties must be assessed, not automatically as alternative legal service providers. The source makes no concrete claim about associate staffing, job losses, market share or access-to-justice outcomes.
